text: Families notice memory change months too late. Clinics test once a year — and the test itself teaches you the test.

This is Lantern. It turns the Alexa already in your kitchen into a gentle early-warning tool — a few short questions through the day, scored against your own normal, and shared with research only if you say so.

Rose is a fictional sixty-eight-year-old. Her mom had Alzheimer's. Nothing here feels like a test — but every answer is a measurement. Delayed recall. Naming animals. Knowing the day. And something new: Lantern remembers what Rose told it yesterday, and checks whether today's story matches.
Under the hood, this page is a real MCP client. Streamable HTTP, spec 2025-11-25, thirteen tools — the same server Alexa+ would call.

Ninety days of Rose. The first two weeks set her personal baseline. Day thirty-eight — she slept three hours and had a rough morning. One bad day. Lantern lets it go, and alarms no one. But from day sixty, her recall and her stories start to slip — a little, every day. Lantern waits for ten straight days before it says anything.
Her daughter Maya, in Seattle, gets one calm email. Not a diagnosis — a nudge. And Alexa finishes the job: it books the doctor visit and sends the invite. Rose never hears the word 'decline.'

For the doctor: one page. Real-change numbers, how often she answered, her sleep, and what Lantern does and doesn't measure. In our demo, Lantern also measures the voice itself, right in the browser: pitch range, speaking speed, pauses. Research shows a flatter voice can appear years before a Parkinson's diagnosis. Alexa+ can't share voice measurements with add-ons yet — that's our number-one request to Amazon.

This is the part for Alzheimer's research. Studies at Penn State and Washington University already show that short, frequent tests at home are reliable — but they need an app and finger taps. Lantern needs nothing new. Researchers enroll a group with a study code, each person gives consent and can quit by voice, and the data exports with names removed, in standard medical formats.
Same server, different assistant — Claude calls it through the Agent Skill. One command runs the whole thing on your own computer.
And if something sudden happens, Lantern says the one thing that matters: call for help, now. Lantern. Not a diagnosis — a reason to talk sooner.

Hi, Rose. Which of the three words do you remember?
Two of three. The other was candle. Now name as many animals as you can.
Eight. Nice! Yesterday you said your granddaughter had a science fair. How did it go?
This could be an emergency. Please call 911 now. I'm letting Maya know.
Want me to book a doctor visit?
